labels.reviewedProbabilities: Reviewed teaching probabilities — not live Qwen output
labels.classroomSelection: Classroom selection demo — not live model inference

actions.incomplete: Complete the four key activities first

page1.title: Several Tokens could come next
page1.subtitle: The model begins with one empty next-token position, not a complete sentence.
page1.question: Is there always only one possible next Token?
page1.intro: The model has combined information from the text so far. It now compares possible Tokens for one next position.
page1.analogy: Like several pieces waiting at one launch gate.
page1.action: Select at least two continuations that could make sense.
page1.feedback: Several Tokens can fit. The model still needs a way to compare them.
page1.takeaway: A language model compares many possible next Tokens.
page1.bridge: The candidates are not all equally likely.

page2.title: Candidates get different chances
page2.subtitle: Reviewed score tracks show how strongly each Token fits this context.
page2.question: How can the model compare possible Tokens?
page2.intro: The processed context produces a numerical score for every possible Token. We can turn scores into chances that add to 100%.
page2.action: Which candidate currently has the highest chance?
page2.highest: Correct. “mat” has the highest reviewed teaching probability.
page2.compareAgain: Compare the printed percentages as well as the ribbon lengths.
page2.takeaway: The same context can give different candidate Tokens different chances.
page2.technical: Real language models first produce numerical scores. A mathematical step turns those scores into probabilities. A high probability is not a feeling of confidence or proof that something is true.
page2.bridge: Scores compare the candidates. A rule must choose one.

page3.title: One rule chooses one Token
page3.subtitle: Highest-chance choice and chance-based choice are two different methods.
page3.question: Must the model always choose the highest chance?
page3.intro: A selection rule turns the candidate chances into one Token. Compare two clear classroom modes.
page3.highestRule: Always choose the current highest chance
page3.chanceRule: Higher chances are more likely, but others remain possible
page3.highestResult: {{token}} was selected because it had the highest reviewed chance.
page3.sampleResult: The fixed classroom sequence selected {{token}} this time.
page3.takeaway: A decoding rule turns candidate chances into one selected Token.
page3.boundary: High probability does not mean factual truth. It only means that a Token fits the learned continuation patterns more strongly in this context.
page3.bridge: The selected Token now joins the text.

page4.title: Add the Token to the text
page4.subtitle: The selected Token becomes part of the context for the next step.
page4.question: What happens after one Token is selected?
page4.intro: The model does not jump to a whole answer. The chosen Token moves into the empty position and the text grows by one piece.
page4.updatedContext: Updated context creates a new empty position
page4.takeaway: The chosen Token becomes part of the next context.
page4.bridge: Now the model can use the updated text to predict again.

page5.title: Predict, add and repeat
page5.subtitle: A longer sentence grows through several one-Token prediction cycles.
page5.question: How can one-Token prediction create longer text?
page5.intro: Use a reviewed starter. Compare the visible candidate chances, select one piece, place it, then repeat with a new candidate set.
page5.discovery: Each selected Token changes the text, so the next set of candidate chances can also change.
page5.takeaway: A language model generates text by predicting, adding and repeating one Token at a time.
page5.boundary: Simplified local candidate tree. This is not full Qwen generation and no model weights are loaded.
page5.bridge: Put the complete one-Token-at-a-time journey together.

page6.title: Your prediction discovery
page6.subtitle: Connect every step from processed context to repeated generation.
page6.question: How does the model create text one Token at a time?
page6.intro: A causal prediction loop compares candidates, selects one Token, updates the context and begins again.
page6.scoresNote: Every possible Token gets a numerical score.
page6.probabilitiesNote: Scores can be shown as chances.
page6.repeatNote: The new context starts another step.
page6.point1: The model compares many possible next Tokens.
page6.point3: Those scores can be represented as probabilities.
page6.point4: A decoding rule chooses one Token.
page6.point5: The chosen Token joins the context.
page6.point6: The process repeats one Token at a time.
page6.accuracy: A likely Token is not automatically true or safe. It only fits the model’s learned patterns for the current context.
page6.next: How did the model learn which patterns should receive higher scores?
